nameStory: Despite its name, the French marigold isn't actually from France at all! This cheerful flower is native to Mexico and Guatemala, but got its "French" label because French gardeners were among the first Europeans to enthusiastically cultivate and develop new varieties of this New World import. The name stuck, even though the plant has never grown wild in France.
description: French marigold is a compact, bushy annual flower that gardeners love for its reliable blooms and easy care. These cheerful plants typically grow 6-12 inches tall and wide, forming neat mounds covered in bright flowers from summer until frost. The flowers come in warm shades of yellow, orange, and red, often with multiple colors on the same bloom. You'll most commonly spot them in gardens, planters, and flower beds throughout New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, ruffled flowers about 1-2 inches across with velvety petals in bright yellows, oranges, and reds, often with darker red markings or edges that create a striped or bicolor effect

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided, feathery green leaves that release a strong, pungent smell when crushed - some people love it, others find it overwhelming and medicinal

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms compact, bushy mounds that stay low to the ground, rarely exceeding 12 inches tall, with multiple stems branching from the base

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Blooms continuously from early summer until the first hard frost, with new flowers constantly replacing spent ones

habitat: In New England, you'll find French marigolds almost exclusively in cultivated settings like home gardens, public flower beds, and container plantings. They prefer full sun and well-drained soil, thriving in the warm, sunny spots that gardeners typically choose for annual flower displays. Occasionally, you might spot them growing as garden escapes near compost piles or in disturbed soil where seeds have scattered.

seasonality.spring: Seeds are planted after the last frost, typically late May in most of New England. Young plants have small, delicate leaves but haven't yet developed their characteristic strong scent.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with continuous flower production. Plants are at their fullest and most fragrant, covered in bright blooms that attract butterflies and other pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming vigorously until the first hard frost kills the plants. Late in the season, you might notice small, dark, needle-like seeds forming if flowers are left to go to seed.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely with frost. Only evidence might be dried stems in neglected garden beds, but most gardeners clean these up in fall preparation.

funFact: French marigolds are nature's pest control specialists - they release chemicals from their roots that actually kill harmful soil nematodes (tiny worms that damage plant roots), which is why smart gardeners plant them near tomatoes and other vegetables as natural bodyguards!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its taller cousin, the Mexican marigold (African marigold), which has much larger flowers (3-4 inches across) and grows 1-3 feet tall. Remember: French marigolds are the short, compact ones with smaller, more delicate flowers, while Mexican marigolds are the tall, bold statement plants.
contextualKnowledge: The marigold naming system is wonderfully confusing - "French" marigolds are from Mexico, "African" marigolds are also from Mexico, and "Mexican mint marigold" is actually from Central America! These common names reflect the complex trade routes and gardening traditions that brought these New World plants to European gardens, not their actual origins.
compareHints: French marigolds are much more compact and delicate than Mexican marigolds, staying under a foot tall compared to their 1-3 foot cousins. The flowers are smaller but often more intricately patterned with multiple colors, while Mexican marigolds tend to be solid-colored giants. French marigolds also have a more refined, bushy growth habit compared to the tall, sometimes gangly Mexican varieties.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Mexican marigolds are significantly larger than French marigolds in every way - taller plants, bigger leaves, and much larger flower heads.
